Starting with 'Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of ', it moves through themes of justice, righteousness and calls readers toward righteousness.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows justice lived out in prosperous but unjust. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come!
“The Lord Yahweh has sworn by himself,” says Yahweh, the God of Armies: “I abhor the pride of Jacob, and detest his fortresses. Therefore I will deliver up the city with all that is in it.
For, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, house of Israel,” says Yahweh, the God of Armies; “and they will afflict you from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.”

questions.question: What is happening in Amos 6?
questions.answer: In 14 verses, this chapter amos 6 (14 verses) continues the story of justice. starting with 'woe to those who are at ease in zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of ', it moves through themes of justice, righteousness and calls readers toward righteousness. The setting is prosperous but unjust, written to northern israel. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Amos and why 6 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally amos, shepherd, addressed to northern israel around ~760 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as oracles — its themes of justice, righteousness build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'righteousness' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Being in right standing, doing what is right. In this chapter, it appears in context of justice. For a first-time reader: think of it as being in right standing, doing what is right, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through justice and righteousness, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 10 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: '“When a man’s relative carries him, even he who burns him, to bring bodies out of the house, and asks him who is in the innermost parts of the house, ‘Is there yet any with you?’ A...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about justice. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
